pulls.title: Implement BIP 54 (Consensus Cleanup) without mainnet activation
pulls.body:
This implements the Consensus Cleanup validation rules proposed in [BIP 54](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0054.md). These rules are only enabled on regtest. Mainnet activation, if any, is to be considered separately.

This patchset is based on the code that was previously reviewed ([1](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/99), [2](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/110)) and tested (for instance [here](https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/consensus-cleanup-demo-of-slow-blocks-on-signet/2367)) on Bitcoin Inquisition. The tests and documentation have since been improved, but the consensus-critical commits have been carried over with only minor differences (the only behavioural one being the addition of the stripped-size check to `PreChecks`).

Roughly 95% of the added lines are tests or test data. The format, contents, and reproduction procedure for the BIP 54 test vectors are documented [here](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/tree/master/bip-0054/test_vectors). The `bip54_tests` unit test module exercises each mitigation extensively in isolation. The `feature_bip54.py` functional test verifies all of them end-to-end after and prior to activation. For the timestamp rules, it simulates timewarp and Murch–Zawy attacks, demonstrating the new timestamp rules prevent these exploits. A fuzz harness for the sigop accounting logic is also included, which can be seeded from the BIP test vectors (implemented [here](https://github.com/darosior/bitcoin/tree/bip54_seed_fuzz_corpus)).

See commit messages for details.

pulls.title: wallet: reject unknown options in sendall
pulls.body:
`sendall` silently ignores unknown keys in its `options` object, including misspelled ones: `input` instead of `inputs` spends all available UTXOs rather than the given ones, and a misspelled `add_to_wallet` or `psbt` can broadcast a transaction the caller asked not to broadcast.

Reject unknown options, like `send`, `fundrawtransaction`, `walletcreatefundedpsbt` and `bumpfee` already do.

pulls.title: refactor: keep duration calculations typed
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Several fixed-duration calculations use raw integer time counts, leaving their units implicit and allowing unrelated integer values to be mixed.

**Fix:** Use `std::chrono` types through calculations where the surrounding APIs already support them, including GUI formatting, peer bans, scheduler forwarding, block timestamps, and target-spacing arithmetic.
Where carrying chrono through an integer interface would broaden the change or make the result harder to read, this PR leaves the expression unchanged or keeps the conversion simply `duration / 1s`.
The remaining integer interfaces receive the same values, and characterization tests pin the PoW timing and inclusive assumevalid threshold.

pulls.title: Contrib: add multisig wizard
pulls.body:
Per the discussion in #35645, this PR adds a Python utility that performs the multisig setup process, so that RPC and interface work is shaped by what that flow actually needs.

It covers wallet creation, key generation at the BIP 87 path, collecting cosigner keys, assembling a `wsh(sortedmulti())` or `tr(musig(),sortedmulti_a())` descriptor, verifying it, and importing it.

### Gaps that need new functionality in C++
- `importdescriptors` rejects a descriptor with no private keys when the wallet has private keys enabled. See #35377.
- The wallet stores a multipath descriptor as two descriptors, so listdescriptors never shows the descriptor that was shared. See #36133.
- The wallet labels addresses, not keys, so cosigner names live in the setup and are lost on import.
- There is no RPC for validating a key expression, so the key is wrapped in `pkh()` for `getdescriptorinfo` to parse. See #35918, which exposes `ParsePubkey()`.
- `createmultisig` only takes plain public keys, not extended keys with origins, and cannot build a ranged or taproot multisig descriptor.
- Nothing reports what a descriptor commits to, or whether this wallet holds one of its keys, before it is imported.

Part of #35645.

pulls.title: net: reimplement private broadcast as jobs isolated from the node
pulls.body:
Split out of #36608, the overall private broadcast rework to support ease of review for like-for-like feature.

Differences from #36608 :
1. No tool support or prep refactors for the tool
2. No package relay
3. Slimmed down test profile focusing on protecting aginst IP address linkage and not crashing the node on adversarial inputs (which is a leak in itself)

With `-privatebroadcast`, `sendrawtransaction` queues a job instead of handing the transaction to
the connection manager. Each job runs on its own thread, shares no state with the node, and
reaches the network only through the Tor proxy: it resolves the chain's DNS seeds, then announces
over BIP324 to recipients on a schedule drawn up front, each connection with fresh isolation
credentials. Nothing a recipient does, and nothing the node sees of the transaction coming back,
changes the plan, and the transaction enters the node's mempool only when it returns from the
network. The old private broadcast connections and relay are removed.

The invariants are specified in `doc/design/private-broadcast.md`.

The rest of the tests are in a follow-up to be considered later:
https://github.com/instagibbs/bitcoin/tree/2026-10-pb_reimpl_followup

pulls.title: net: reject oversized outbound messages
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Outbound transports encode message types in a fixed 12-byte field, but `CConnman` did not ensure internal callers respected this limit before queuing messages.
An oversized type aborts V1 encoding. V2 sends it under a truncated type with its payload intact, or writes past its encoding buffer when the payload is shorter than the excess type bytes.
The send path also did not enforce the 4 MB payload limit.

**Fix:** Treat oversized types and payloads as failed assumptions in `CConnman::PushMessage()` before they enter the send queue.

pulls.title: descriptor: Expose key expression parsing
pulls.body:
This PR exposes a utility function to parse and validate a standalone descriptor key expression. 
This is particularly useful in GUI multisig setup flows where the UI accepts a pasted key expression. The GUI can use this parser to validate input, inspect the parsed key,  and apply setup-specific policy i.e. reject private keys, uncompressed keys etc. (Multisig Wizard tracking issue: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/35645)

`PubkeyProvider` is the existing internal representation of a parsed key expression. This PR exposes its interface in `descriptor.h` and adds a public `ParsePubkey()` overload that returns the providers produced by the existing parser.

Key changes
- public overload uses P2TR key rules, permitting compressed, x-only, extended, and MuSig key expressions while rejecting uncompressed keys.
- Add `GetOriginInfo()` for retrieving explicitly provided key origin information.

---
Also, while I'm here, I noticed that `musig` parser accepted trailing characters apart from `/`. 
- Add a fix & test to reject unexpected trailing characters after a `musig()` expression

pulls.title: Add output script index and corresponding script history RPC
pulls.body:
Add a new index `txoscriptindex` which indexes all output scripts. Introduce a new `getscripthistory` RPC that returns all transactions that create outputs corresponding to the provided scripts, and optionally the transactions that spend those outputs if `txospenderindex` is also configured.

This has been a long-requested feature, attempted in previous PRs (#2802, #3652, #6835, #10370, #14053).
Some concerns raised were about the ability for an index like this to scale. I think the new techniques being used to build the indexes (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35531, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36002) alleviate this concern. This index can be synced in a few hours and the current disk usage is ~52 GB. This is less than the ~66 GB `txindex` disk usage in v31 and earlier. This index can also be used with a pruned node, so a full node can be supported in < 100 GB of disk space. Missing blocks are returned by hash and can be requested from peers using `getblockfrompeer`.

Some other previous concerns were more conceptual, that this type of index could encourage address reuse and chain analysis. IMO this ship has sailed, and the current status quo of not shipping an address index is turning off users who expect this functionality. Workarounds involve installing, configuring, and syncing other third-party software, making the UX of using Bitcoin Core in a self-sovereign way unnecessarily difficult.

The index hashes each output script with SHA256, then applies salted SipHash-1-3-UJ and stores a five-byte prefix. This is to support the popular Electrum protocol, which supplies only the script hash. The RPC can also look up by address or descriptors. Ranged descriptors are also supported, so a single RPC call can return the entire history of a receive/change xpub pair.

Because there are some scripts with millions of outputs, we introduce a new `OrderedVarInt` which serializes the block height after the script hash prefix. This lets LevelDB seek directly to the prefix + block height, so we can page by block height range.

To prevent DoS concerns by supplying an address with millions of outputs, the RPC tracks a byte budget of reads and throws immediately if too many reads are attempted. The error message instructs the user to narrow the block range.

Improvements to `txospenderindex` (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36480) will also allow us to use that pruned. The end result would allow users to run with all optional indexes (including this one) in < 200 GB of disk space. Of course a larger pruned setting would be desired if many historical block lookups were being requested.

pulls.title: validation: prefetch blocks while connecting
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Connecting a block already on disk requires reading and deserializing it.
Doing this on the validation thread stalls validation and slows reindexing and initial block download.

This is a follow-up to [#35295](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35295), which parallelized input prevout fetching during block connection.

**Fix:** Add a `Chainstate`-owned block fetcher that reads later blocks from disk while the current block is connected.
Start with synchronous 1-block read-ahead, then move reads to an eagerly started worker pool that persists across activations.
Keep caller-provided blocks on the direct path and refill a sliding read-ahead window.
During reorgs, start reading the first sibling while disconnecting the old tip.
Retry speculative failures synchronously when the block is needed.

`-blockfetchthreads=<n>` selects readers per chainstate, with a default of 2 and a cap of 16.
Setting it to 0 disables read-ahead. The window retains up to two blocks per reader, giving 4 by default.
Measurements favor 2 readers with a window of 4 or 8 blocks, so the default uses the smaller window.

**Credit:** The idea comes from [bitcoindev1337](https://bitcoin-irc.chaincode.com/bitcoin-core-dev/2026-08-11#1245429), who had already implemented a similar design and reported comparable results.

pulls.title: txindex: allow running in pruned mode
pulls.body:
After #35531, each txindex entry now points to the block hash containing the tx instead of the file location of the block. The block hash is then used to find the file position of the block to read the tx from. This allows us to determine the hash of the containing block even if the block is later pruned, and also determine the location of the block on disk if it is later downloaded again via `getblockfrompeer`.

This PR enables maintaining a txindex while pruned. If a txid lookup tries to read a tx from a pruned block, the hash of the missing block is surfaced to the caller.

If desired, a user may call `getblockfrompeer` using the returned hash to download the block, then try again successfully. The downloaded block will be added to the front of the block queue, so won't be pruned again for at least 288 blocks. Of course a larger prune setting is desired if lots of historical blocks will be read, and there are privacy issues if the user is looking up their own transactions. Ideally the blocks can be fetched from a trusted node or from random peers with decoy blocks fetched occasionally.

Resolves https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/10609, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/12651, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/16182, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/35240

pulls.title: net: receive TCP urgent data inline
pulls.body:
There is currently nothing preventing us to receive TCP urgent data, which would never be returned by `recv()`. Linux's `poll()` is indifferent to this, but the `select()` socket monitoring may keep reporting it as pending on some platforms.

This would not prevent progress nor lead to a crash anymore after #36665, but it's still undesirable. Clean this up by setting `SO_OOBINLINE` on our sockets, so `recv()` returns any urgent data sent to us (and likely leads us to disconnect the peer).

This is a slight behaviour change on Linux, but i think a desirable one. First of all because if a peer is sending us funky data we might as well hear about it and disconnect them, but also because i think one lesson to draw from the recent [socket related security vulnerability](https://bitcoincore.org/en/2026/10/28/disclose-tcp-oom/) is that we should reduce the amount of custom logic for less well-tested platforms.

Failing to set `SO_OOBINLINE` was conservatively made a warning and not a failure, because its absence does not prevent node operations, it's just annoying.

pulls.title: txorphanage: bound orphan memory by storing transactions serialized
pulls.body:
The orphanage limits the "usage" of the orphans it stores, per peer and globally, to bound the amount of memory an attacker can make us hold on to. It uses weight as a proxy for that memory, on the assumption that weight is "often higher than the actual memory usage of the transaction".

That assumption does not hold for a deserialized transaction. Every witness stack element is an individually heap-allocated vector, costing its 24-byte slot in the stack vector plus a 32-byte minimum allocation, while only weighing 2WU. A transaction of 199,000 1-byte witness elements weighs 398,247WU (i.e. it is of standard weight, and witness standardness cannot be checked while the inputs are missing), but uses 11.1MB of memory: 28 times what is accounted for it, and one such orphan can be retained per peer.

Rather than change the accounting metric, keep orphans in serialized form, deserializing them again on the paths that hand them back out. Serialized, a transaction's memory usage is bounded by its weight, so the existing weight-based accounting becomes a true upper bound on memory and the worst case is the peers' combined allowances.

Admission, eviction and accounting behavior are unchanged: no transaction that was previously accepted is refused, so orphan resolution (and thus 1p1c package relay) keeps working for standard-weight transactions whose witnesses consist of many small elements, such as BitVM-style transactions.

pulls.title: [wip,nomerge,rfc] build: Require C++23 compiler
pulls.body:
C++23 for Bitcoin Core is mostly a "style update" on top of C++20. However, the workarounds to avoid C++23 keep accumulating and some parts of the code already use C++23 features, such as lambda attributes (https://github.com/bitcoin-core/libmultiprocess/commit/bdd0cd69418d189f62699d274a751cbf6d36bb43).

I don't know when it is fine to switch, but at some point, I think it is fine to require a C++23 compiler, so that [new stuff](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/34979#issuecomment-4448399166) is unlocked. Of course this requires bumping the minimum required compiler versions:

* GCC: 13
* Clang: 19

There are some C++23 features that aren't implemented (such as `<stacktrace>` not really shipped in any vanilla stdlib today), or e.g. `ranges::starts_with` not implemented until libstdc++-16. But overall I think we are better off using C++23 without those few features instead of waiting longer?

pulls.title: build: Bump g++ minimum supported version to 13
pulls.body:
At some point, it may be fine to [drop support for older vanilla systems](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/34979) not shipping with at least GCC 13.

(For this bump, only C++20 `std::format` will become available, but this bump should also pave the way for C++23.)

This patch will only be released in version 33.x, or later, next year (2027).

For reference:

* https://packages.ubuntu.com/noble/g++ (g++-13)
* https://packages.debian.org/trixie/g++ (g++-14)
* CentOS-like 8/9/10 ship recent GCC via appstream (`dnf install -y gcc-toolset-15`)
* Free/Open/Net*BSD ship a recent GCC
* OpenSuse Leap and Tumbleweed ship with g++ 15 https://software.opensuse.org/package/gcc15-c++

On operating systems where the minimum GCC version is not shipped by default, the user would have to use Clang, or install GCC in a different way. For example:

* Debian Bookworm could use https://packages.debian.org/bookworm/clang-22
* Ubuntu 22.04 would have to use a general alternative:
* [PPA](https://launchpad.net/~ubuntu-toolchain-r/+archive/ubuntu/test), https://apt.llvm.org/ (for Clang), brew, nix, guix, or compile GCC from source, ...

Obviously, downloading pre-compiled releases or compiling previous release branches is unaffected by this change.

pulls.title: http: support unix sockets
pulls.body:
Closes https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/5029

Accept unix socket paths as options for `-rpcbind=` (server) and `-rpcconnect=` (bitcoin-cli). Options follow the same pattern as `ipcbind`:

- `=unix` is a magic keyword that means `<datadir>/http.sock`
- `=unix:relative/path` means `<datadir>/relative/path`
- `=unix:/absolute/path` means `/absolute/path`

We delete any existing `http.sock` before calling `bind()` and do not clean up at shutdown.

Because access is handled by the filesystem, `-rpcallowip` is ignored for unix sockets and not required at all if we are *only* binding to unix sockets.

Authentication by username/password/cookie is still required.

A new option `--httpunix` is added to the test framework and added to test_runner for `rpc_bind.py` and `interface_http.py` for CI, but (like `--usecli`) most other tests should also pass with that option. When set, bitcoind is started with `-rpcbind=unix...`which overrides `tcp://localhost` entirely. `AuthProxy` has been extended to connect directly to the unix socket.

Try it out!
```
bitcoind -regtest -rpcbind=unix
bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcconnect=unix getbestblockhash
```

Refactored code:

Back in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/27375 we added unix socket support but it was isloated to the `Proxy` class. That created a bit of tech debt which we pay off in this PR. Two new classes are implemented:
- `UnixSocketAddr` reflects the `CService` API for generic unix sockets, without bitcoin-p2p-specific attributes
- `SocketAddr` holds a variant of `UnixSocketAddr` and `Cservice` so classes like `Proxy` and `HTTPServer` can operate on an abstract level, with either socket type.
- `CNetAddr` and `CService` are left untouched -- they are somewhat dirty combinations of generic socket classes and bitcoin p2p code, adding unix sockets to those classes wouldn't make sense for bitcoin p2p operations and that's why this design was chosen.

Follow-up suggestions:
- Deduplicate some of the unix socket path resolution code between IPC and HTTP
- On macos the default unix socket buffer size is only ~8k. In the functional tests we have to bump the python client socket buffer up to ~256k or the "throttle" tests will stall on macos. We could apply this socket option on the server side as well, only on macos... requires some bike shedding.
- This option replaces TCP but it does not replace HTTP, there may be a more efficient transport protocol.


Production code and test framework changes designed and authored by my own cranial meatball. Unit tests added by Opus. C++ cleaned up by Fable, security tightened by Kimi-k3 🧠 🤖 🤖 🤖

pulls.title: mining: move getblocktemplate cache into BlockTemplateManager
pulls.body:
Follow-up to #35675. This addresses the `getblocktemplate` part of the "Remove remaining global states" TODO in #33758, as suggested in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35675#pullrequestreview-5299625960.

`getblocktemplate` reuses its last template until the tip changes, or until the mempool changes and the template is more than 5 seconds old. That cache currently lives in four function-local statics, which:

- live as long as the process, so the cached `CBlockIndex*` can outlive its `ChainstateManager` (as in unit tests);
- rely on `cs_main` being held, which nothing checks;
- can't be unit tested.

This PR moves the cache into `BlockTemplateManager`, in three commits:

1. **rpc:** refactors the statics in place into a `CachedBlockTemplate` struct and a `GetNewOrCachedBlockTemplate()` helper, `GUARDED_BY(::cs_main)`. The template's `hashPrevBlock` replaces the cached `CBlockIndex*`, and the 5 seconds becomes `GBT_TEMPLATE_REBUILD_INTERVAL`.
2. **refactor:** moves them into `BlockTemplateManager`. It's easiest to review with `git show --color-moved=dimmed-zebra --color-moved-ws=allow-indentation-change`.
3. **test:** adds a unit test for each rebuild rule and for the retry after a failed build.

No behavior change is intended, and only `getblocktemplate` uses the cache. It uses `cs_main` rather than its own mutex, since the RPC already holds it and building a template takes it anyway.

pulls.title: net: serve `MSG_BLOCK` by stripping witnesses in place
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Serving blocks to legacy nodes currently decodes and reserializes them just to remove witnesses. `MSG_WITNESS_BLOCK` already avoids this work by serving the stored bytes directly. Faster witnessless IBD, as proposed in [#36476](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36476), also needs peers to serve these blocks efficiently.

**Fix:** Read disk-backed, non-Signet `MSG_BLOCK` replies into an owned byte buffer, check the header's proof of work and expected hash, and strip witness ranges from that buffer in place.

Extract a shared helper so decoding transactions and skipping their bytes follow the same encoding rules. Signet keeps `ReadBlock` for its solution check. Header checks now precede transaction parsing, so records corrupted in both places can log a different error.

**Performance:**

Time to read a block from disk and build its non-witness message:

| Block | Before | After | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `block413567` | 1.31 ms | 0.147 ms | **8.9x** |
| Same block with synthetic witnesses | 3.47 ms | 0.374 ms | **9.3x** |

The synthetic fixture adds a 512-byte witness item and an empty item to every input.

**Related work:** This extends the raw witness-block serving added in [#13151](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13151). The [#13011 discussion](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13011#issuecomment-383145046) and the closed [#13098](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/13098) identify unnecessary transaction hashing when serving historical blocks. The implementation also builds on the bulk block reads introduced in [#31551](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31551).

Add goals for selected high-value paths, including IBD and non-IBD message processing, completed P2P handshakes and transport messages, successful estimator/mempool/snapshot operations, transaction and package acceptance, and compact block reconstruction.

Built the fuzz binary and replayed the current qa-assets corpora for all instrumented targets with `FUZZ_ENFORCE_REACHABILITY=1`.

pulls.title: validation: return block-file flush errors
pulls.body:
**Problem:** When flushing block or undo data fails, `FlushStateToDisk()` still writes block-index metadata and coins data, then advances `m_last_flushed_block`.
With a separate `-blocksdir`, persistent failures there can leave metadata referring to block data that is not durable even when chainstate writes succeed.

**Fix:** Return the flush error before those writes, leaving the last-flushed marker and on-disk coins tip unchanged in the failing call.
Later flushes can retry and write if they succeed, including during shutdown.
`ConnectTip()` and `DisconnectTip()` propagate the error before updating the chain tip, after applying the coins changes in memory.

**History:**
* [#27866](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/27866#discussion_r1297313148) raised whether saving other state after a flush failure was preferable. This change preserves later retries while skipping writes in the failing call.
* [#34897](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34897) introduced `m_last_flushed_block` to prevent persistent indexes from advancing past flushed chainstate. This fix keeps it at the last successful flush.

pulls.title: test: check guarantees of bech32 error detection
pulls.body:
This adds bech32 checks around the limits of bech32 strings, and the guarantees, as well as the limitations, of bech error detection.

The first commit adds those tests:
- validity of a bech32 string at the base max length, and invalidity after that
- validity of a bech32 string at the length limit for silent payment addresses (1023)
- failing checksums after 1-4 changes for length 90
- show that after 5 changes another valid checksum might exist
- failing checksum after 1-3 changes for length 1023
- show that after 4 changes another valid checksum might exist
- Show that LocateErrors can locate up to 2 errors
- Show that LocateErrors might locate a different solution to get a valid checksum

Second commit just modifies comments about error detection 'guarantees' around bech32 length limit constants. I think the formulation 'Guarantees finding up to N errors' is ambiguous.
Someone might interpret it as 'fixes up to N errors', but it's not. It's not even 'Locates up to N errors', since LocateErrors() can find up to 2 errors. Now with the new 1023 length, LocateError can't even anymore guarantee finding the correct 2 errors (2 errors in one direction, 2 changes tried in the other direction, and we are beyond the 3 changes that guarantee there is no other possible valid checksum).
So I think the comments should only say 'The checksum can detect up to N changes' instead, not guarantee more.

Context : 
Initially I was just looking at all code around Silent Payments, looked if the bech32 test had been updated to have tests for the new CharLimit::SILENT_PAYMENTS, and saw less tests than I expected.

**Problem:** Test helpers that attach active-tip templates to arbitrary parents retain the template's subsidy.

pulls.title: wallet: harden external signer psbt processing, revamp mock
pulls.body:
The current external signer functional test mock can only echo a prepared PSBT. This gets in the way of testing more complicated scenarios, i.e. misbehaving signers and (MuSig2) multisig.

- *test: have external signer mock use a wallet*: gives the mock its own offline node and wallet with private keys, while the test uses the watch-only version.
- *external_signer: require matching PSBT versions*
- *external_signer: merge PSBT response instead of replacing*: tests signers that drop outputs, reduce their value or change the script. Merging rejects these changes while allowing signers to omit unnecessary PSBT fields.
- *external_signer: reject unsafe sighash types*
- *external_signer: **reject finalized PSBT inputs***: keeps the above check simple. Documents this new requirement. HWI does not finalize.

The remaining commits prepare the test helpers and enforce IWYU for `src/external_signer.cpp`.

This PR absorbs the scenarios from #35358, but is better able to test them thanks to the new mock signer implementation.

This PR does not intend to fully harden against a malicious external signer, and can't protect against a malicious HWI (equivalent) process running as the same user.

cli: Parse -signetchallenge like bitcoind
pulls.body:
`bitcoind` returns an useful error when invalid hex is passed to `-signetchallenge`:

```
$ bitcoind -signet -signetchallenge=z
Error: -signetchallenge must be hex, not 'z'
```

The error returned by `bitcoin-cli` only indicates that the RPC cookie wasn't found. It doesn't hint at invalid hex:

```
$ bitcoin-cli -signet -signetchallenge=z getblockcount
error: Authorization failed: ...
Is your -signetchallenge correct for custom signets?
```

To have consistent validation of signet args in `bitcoind` and `bitcoin-cli`, we now parse `-signetchallenge` in a new `ReadSigNetChallengeArg()` function which is called in `ReadSigNetDir()` and `ReadSigNetArgs()`.

Addresses https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34566#discussion_r3668123074

pulls.title: Indexes: Harden the flush-error notification invariant
pulls.body:
This is a follow-up to #35714 as it has the two commits of that PR, do not merge or review before that PR

#35714 makes `FlushStateToDisk()` return `state.Error(...)` when `FlushChainstateBlockFile()` fails, relying on the comment `// FlushChainstateBlockFile() already emitted the flush-error notification.`

That invariant holds today, but it is not guaranteed by construction: it depends on every `success = false` branch inside `FlushBlockFile`/`FlushUndoFile` emitting the notification on its own. A future flush source (a new file type, a new error branch) that sets `success = false` **without** notifying would make `FlushStateToDisk()` return an error without `AbortNode()`.

This PR makes sure that **whenever a flush reports failure, the flush-error notification has been emitted**:

- **test: cover FlushBlockFile flush-error notifications**: lower-level `BlockManager` tests (as suggested in the #35714 review) that inject a failure on the block file and on the undo file separately and assert each failure emits `flushError`.
- **blockstorage: encapsulate flush+notify in FlushFile**:  a single `FlushFile()` helper couples the flush and the notification; `FlushBlockFile`/`FlushUndoFile` delegate to it. Behaviour is unchanged.

pulls.title: fuzz: add a custom mutator for PSBT
pulls.body:
The `partially_signed_transaction_deserialize` target feeds raw bytes to the PSBT parser. Byte-level mutations rarely produce well-formed key-value maps with valid keydata (pubkeys, xpubs, control blocks, DER signatures, etc), so most inputs are rejected early and the deeper per-field parsing is rarely reached.

This PR adds a custom mutator for PSBT which is ported from bitcoinfuzz (with some changes).  The mutator splits the input into global/input/output maps of key-value records, applies the mutations and serializes the result again. The first commit is a preparation to allow targets to provide a custom mutator by adding an optional `mutator` field to
`FuzzTargetOptions`. 

note: LLM assisted on porting the custom mutator.

pulls.title: net: enforce timeout interval for paused send peers

I picked 20 minutes as the reasonable time frame, since it's what we already use for ping timeouts today.

pulls.title: descriptor, rpc, wallet: do not echo key material in error messages
pulls.body:
Some descriptor error messages quote the string the caller sent, and a descriptor can hold a private key (a WIF, an xprv). The reply then carries the key into places the request may not go: an application's error log, an error reporter, a screenshot shared for help. Even the first characters of a key give away part of it.

This PR stops the quoting.

**Parsing** (`descriptor.cpp`, `util/bip32.cpp`):

| before | after |
| --- | --- |
| `Key ' <key>' is invalid due to whitespace` | `Key is invalid due to whitespace` |
| `key '<key>' is not valid` | `key is not valid` |
| `Pubkey '<hex>' is invalid` | `Pubkey is invalid` |
| `Multi threshold '<text>' is not valid` | same for text of 11 characters or fewer, the length of `4294967295h`; `Multi threshold is not valid` for longer text |
| `Key path value '<text>' specifies multipath in a section where multipath is not allowed` | same rule: `Key path value specifies multipath in a section where multipath is not allowed` for longer text |
| `Key path value '<text>' is not a valid uint32` | same rule: `Key path value is not a valid uint32` for longer text |
| `'<expr>' is not a valid descriptor function` | `'<name>(...' is not a valid descriptor function`, where `<name>` is the text up to `(`; `Not a valid descriptor function` if there is no `(` or the name is longer than 16 characters |

No key is 11 characters or fewer.

**Callers**:

- `Cannot derive script without private keys: '...'` (`rpc/util.cpp`) and `Could not add descriptor '...': ...` (`wallet/imports.cpp`) now quote `desc->ToString()`, the public form with its checksum.
- `Unable to parse descriptor '...': ...` (`wallet/rpc/spend.cpp`) no longer quotes the string: there is no parsed descriptor to print, and the parse error says what is wrong.

Existing assertions on these messages are updated. New tests check that no part of a key is in the parse errors and the caller errors, including a key with a typo in its last character. They also check the exact text of the caller errors.

This is one of several PRs from a large audit of Bitcoin Core that I did with the help of LLM tools. The audit produced its evidence all at once, which is why the PRs arrive together. I understand each change fully and will answer review questions myself.

pulls.title: refactor: Use std::erase and std::erase_if
pulls.body:
Convert `remove` and `remove_if` to the C++20 `std::erase` and `std::erase_if` overloads.

The legacy ones can be confusing, because:

* Array-based containers (like vector) must use the erase-remove idiom. Forgetting the erase, or forgetting to pass the end iterator (`bugprone-inaccurate-erase`) can be a bug, see also https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36588#discussion_r4345799022. So a call only to "remove" will not erase.
* Node-based containers (like list or set) must not use the idiom. Using it will be a pessimization or won't compile. And correctly not using the idiom reads confusing, because a call to "remove" will actually erase.
* They are more verbose.

Also convert simple iterator-erase (which is verbose, but fine) to the std overload.

pulls.title: net: validate Tor onion service replies and cached keys
pulls.body:
**Problem:** A node creates its onion service through Tor's control protocol and caches the returned `PrivateKey` value for reconnects.
Tor reply parsing unescapes quoted values, so a control endpoint can return a value containing a line break or space.
On reconnect, the node inserts that value unquoted into an `ADD_ONION` command.
CRLF frames the remainder as a separate command, while a space adds further arguments.
An unprivileged local process can exploit this by impersonating the default loopback endpoint while Tor is unavailable, seeding the cache, and releasing the port before Tor is available again.
A compromised operator-configured endpoint can return the same malicious value.
The reply handler also continues after receiving an invalid service ID, logging it and caching the key before attempting to advertise the invalid address.
A later reply without a service ID can reuse an ID left by an earlier reply.

**Fix:** This PR validates the returned service ID as a Tor v3 onion address before logging it, caching the key, or advertising the service.
Each reply must provide its own service ID, and reply fields stay local until validation succeeds.
Key validation accepts `NEW:ED25519-V3` or an `ED25519-V3` key whose Base64 payload decodes to 64 bytes.
Returned keys are validated before adoption or caching, and cached keys are validated before reuse.
A malformed cached key leaves the onion service unavailable until the operator removes the file and restarts the node. It cannot inject another command or argument.

pulls.title: Reimplement private broadcast as node state-less jobs + package relay support
pulls.body:
## Goals

Goal 1: Remove reliance on, and probes about, internal node state from private broadcast

Goal 2: Specify observable behavior to aid reimplementation and reduce profile fingerprints across versions

### Layout

Four parts, each starting with an empty marker commit:

1. support: moves shared code into the common library; no behavior change
2. bitcoin-privbcast: the specification and the standalone tool
3. bitcoind -privatebroadcast as jobs: the node runs the tool's job; the old relay and connections are removed
4. package mode: one parent and its child. Its validation commits (saturating fee sum, test-accept as submission, self-paying parent) serve only this part.

For the v33 release, I think 1 through 3 should be the goal, but the roadmap could be trimmed down to remove tool-only code if the conceptual support for the standalone tool is not there.

The tool itself introduces about 600 loc of logic, and also necessitates some of the prep move-only commits putting things in common. The vast majority is the shared Job machinery.


## Node-less state

The primary failure mode of the in-master private broadcast is that it relies on node state for operation, and this has led to a number of "careful coding" fixes:

1. The v2->v1 retry connected directly, without the proxy: #35319 (merged in #35410)
2. Discouraging a misbehaving peer gave a clearnet oracle: #36312
3. Eager job completion via mempool inspection: #36277
4. Private broadcast connections wrote to addrman: #35032

There are many other sources of fingerprints as well, some harder than others to exploit, and to fix. The solution: remove reliance on node state entirely to drive attempts. The spec states the goals as:

- A job reveals neither the sender's IP address, onion address nor node identity to any party.
- A hostile recipient, DNS seed or Tor exit learns no more than an honest one. It can only affect delivery.

### Jobs, slots and opportunities

- **Job**: one broadcast of one transaction, from submission to its report. A job spends its first 12 s finding candidates (IPv4/IPv6 addresses from the DNS seeds, resolved through Tor exits), then delivers. It runs for at most 10 min.
- **Slot**: one of a job's 6 independent delivery targets. Each slot tries to announce the transaction to one peer and serve it when asked. Slots 0–2 open when delivery starts; slot 3 opens 35–180 s later; slots 4–5 open 185–240 s later, at least 5 s apart. Each of these times is drawn at random within its range.
- **Opportunity**: one of a slot's 4 scheduled connection times: a first attempt and up to 3 fallbacks, each 50–60 s after the previous. A fallback runs only if the slot's previous attempt failed before announcing; once a slot announces, its remaining opportunities are dropped.

The times are drawn at job start, and each opportunity's candidate is fixed when discovery ends, before any peer is contacted. Nothing a peer does moves them (C1–C4). A job makes at most 24 connections, at most 6 of them at once.

### Differences at a glance

| | master | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Where it runs | Inside `bitcoind` only | `bitcoind -privatebroadcast`, or the standalone `bitcoin-privbcast` with no node; the same job either way (U3), with a JSON report of every connection |
| Recipients | `addrman.Select()` over onion, I2P, and IPv4/IPv6 through the proxy; networks follow `-onlynet` | DNS seed names resolved through Tor exits (RESOLVE), IPv4/IPv6 only; no node state used (R1, R6) |
| Connections | `CConnman` peers of type `PRIVATE_BROADCAST`, visible in `getpeerinfo` | The job's own proxy streams, each with fresh SOCKS credentials, so each gets its own circuit; not peers of the node |
| Plan | 3 connections, then more whenever the tx is stale (5 min, then 1 min) until it comes back from the network | 6 slots of 4 opportunities, all scheduled at job start; no retries; at most 10 min |
| Transport | v2 when addrman advertises it, otherwise v1, with a v2→v1 retry | BIP324 v2 only, with one constant VERSION per release (B4, E1) |
| Node settings | Shape which networks and peers are used | Peer-selection settings don't apply to jobs (U2) |
| Packages | — | `submitpackage` with one parent and one child: announce the child, serve the parent on request |

### No addrman

Under master, the node's private broadcast destinations are drawn from the node's addrman. Other parties write to that table through addr gossip, which makes it a unique fingerprint vector, and inherently attacker influenced. This rules out drawing recipients from anything the node or its peers can write to.

Its replacement is querying DNS seeds in a predetermined way under a static profile. This is inherently less robust than the p2p network in terms of liveness, but leaves no fingerprint within a release. The marginal fingerprint is the set of DNS seeds per release, which affects who is queried and exactly how. Each RESOLVE returns one address and exits cache answers, so each seed is asked through several exits: 4 Tor circuits, each querying all 7 seeds, for up to 28 results, which are assigned to the 6x4 opportunities before any dialing happens. A circuit per query, 28 in all, kept Tor busy enough that overlapping discoveries lost answers.

If the list shrinks, grows, or is modified, the release is revealed to the Tor exits carrying the queries, which see every seed name queried. A DNS seed learns only that it is on the list, and only when the exit has no cached answer.

The fingerprint potential also precludes fixed seeds, which change greatly each release, and which degrade in connectivity over time regardless.

### Minimal release fingerprint

Once a release is cut, behavior profiles are intended to be identical per user. This precludes user knobs and per-instance parameters, and requires a constant user agent and VERSION.

Across releases, the reimplemented p2p message state machine allows better control of unnecessary profile breaks going forward.

### Specification

`doc/design/private-broadcast-tool.md` comes before any code in part 2. It has goals, a threat model per party (recipient, exit, seed, network observer, guard), 54 numbered invariants (A–U, N), parameters, interface, assumptions, non-goals and a rationale. Code comments and tests cite the invariant IDs, so review can check code against a stated property. Concept review of the goals, threat model and non-goals is most useful first, then review of the implementation against the invariants.

This implementation is actually the second implementation, initially implemented solely via the spec and black box tests, which were handed to an otherwise blind agent.

### Tradeoffs

- Needs Tor, including Tor's RESOLVE extension. I2P is gone, and so are onion recipients. To re-add these, we need a connect->GETADDR step, and then have to filter out most of the addresses that do not answer when dialed.
- DNS seeds and Tor exits learn that a job ran, in addition to end recipients.
- No retries beyond the scheduled fallbacks. Retrying would act on whether the transaction comes back, which the adversary controls; the user resubmits instead.
- `getprivatebroadcastinfo` now reports jobs, and the connections no longer show in `getpeerinfo`.

pulls.title: psbt: verify final scripts in FinalizePSBT
pulls.body:
`finalizepsbt` can return `complete: true` and a hex for a PSBT whose `PSBT_IN_FINAL_SCRIPTWITNESS` (or final scriptSig) is invalid.

`FinalizePSBT` counts an input as complete when `SignPSBTInput` succeeds. If the input already has final fields, `PSBTInput::FillSignatureData` marks the sigdata complete and `ProduceSignature` returns true early (sign.cpp:752), before the script is verified. So the existing final fields are trusted as-is.

To reproduce, take a signed P2WPKH v0 PSBT that has a `non_witness_utxo` and flip one bit of the signature inside the final witness:
- `finalizepsbt` returns `complete: true` and a hex
- `analyzepsbt` says the input is not final, `next: finalizer`
- `testmempoolaccept` on the hex fails with `mempool-script-verify-flag-failed (Signature must be zero for failed CHECK(MULTI)SIG operation)`

Inputs that only have a `witness_utxo` already come out incomplete because of the `require_witness_sig` check, so this affects inputs with a `non_witness_utxo`.

#30357 fixed the same problem in `FillPSBT` by checking `PSBTInputSignedAndVerified`, and #33014 did it for `descriptorprocesspsbt`. This does the same in `FinalizePSBT`. Taproot verification needs every spent output. If one is missing, that input already fails in `SignPSBTInput` with `MISSING_INPUTS` and makes the PSBT incomplete, so the extra check doesn't change the result in that case.

The new test in `rpc_psbt.py` builds that PSBT and checks that `finalizepsbt` returns `complete: false` with no hex. It fails on master and passes with the fix. `wallet_musig.py` and the `psbt_wallet_tests` / `script_tests` unit tests still pass.

One behaviour change: a final script that is valid by consensus but non-standard now gives `complete: false`. `FillPSBT` and `descriptorprocesspsbt` already behave that way, since they check with the same standard flags.

pulls.title: test: Check bitcoin wrapper child exit status on windows
pulls.body:
Follow-up to #36105, which makes the Windows `bitcoin.exe` wrapper wait for its child and forward the child's exit code. This adds the functional test for that.

The case worth covering is exit code -1. The first version of the wrapper used `_spawnvp(_P_WAIT)`, which returns -1 both when the spawn fails and when the child started fine and exited with -1, so `bitcoin.exe` reported a startup error and exited 1 instead of passing -1 through. #36105 now uses `_P_NOWAIT` + `_cwait`, which keeps the spawn result and the child status separate. Against the old launcher this test fails at `not(1 == 4294967295)`.

The test copies `bitcoin.exe` into a temp dir next to a copy of `cmd.exe` named `bitcoind.exe`, so `bitcoin -M node /d /c exit N` runs the fake child, and checks 0, 1 and -1 come back unchanged. Windows reports exit codes as unsigned 32-bit, so -1 arrives as 4294967295. It also checks the wrapper adds nothing to stdout/stderr. The exit code test is Windows only.

ryanofsky preferred keeping the runtime fix in #36105 and reviewing the test here (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36190#issuecomment-5603692520), so this is the same commit he briefly carried in his branch. The branch still contains #36105's commits and should land after it.

Checked on a native Windows 11 clang/UCRT release build, wallet/GUI/IPC off:

```text
cmake --build build --target bitcoin bitcoind bitcoin-cli
python test/functional/tool_bitcoin.py --configfile=build/test/config.ini --tmpdir=build/tool-bitcoin-exit-status
```

Fails against the pre-fix launcher, passes against the fixed one, and the rest of `tool_bitcoin.py` still passes. Use a fresh `--tmpdir` when re-running.

pulls.title: private broadcast: Extra guard against unintended non-private broadcast of private transactions
pulls.body:
Motivation: Reduce the risk of accidental privacy leak happening when broadcasting non-privately a requested transaction that had been previously broadcast privately.

Background: During the initial phase of private broadcast implementation there were unforeseen instances when a private transaction could get broadcast non-privately (see #35032 #35319 #35410 #36309 #36312 #36277 #36330).

Currently known pathways:

- Re-submission through `submitpackage`
- Wallet-rebroadcast (when a private transaction is "picked up" by the wallet, and rebrodcast after 1-2 days)

Note that these are being addressed, but other, currently non-identified pathways cannot be excluded.

Change summary: Add a general, extra safeguard: whenever there is a transaction broadcast request, check if the given transaction has been previously broadcast privately, and if so, refuse to broadcast non-privately.

Transaction relay is not affected, as it should not be affected by private broadcast.  When we receive a previously private-broadcast transaction for the first time (it's not yet in our mempool), we relay it as any other relayed transaction. Behavior is unchanged in this regard.

Notes:

- Prerequisite: This is built on top of #36477, as keeping finished private broadcasts in the queue is a prerequisite for this change to work.
- This proposed change is not an alternative to the use-case specific safeguards, but a complementary one.
- Testing currently uses the two pathways listed above. When they are closed, testing will be more difficult (i.e., it is hard to establish whether non-private broadcast is prevented by the use-case specific or the present generic guard).
- The private broadcast queue is not persisted, it doesn't survive node restarts
- Entries deleted via `abortprivatebroadcast` will be forgotten.

Keeping as Draft, because the prerequisite #36477 is pending.

pulls.title: contrib: fix dead null-byte check in linearize-data.py
pulls.body:
`linearize-data.py` hangs on any block file that ends in zero padding.

Reproduce:

```
mkdir -p /tmp/lin/blocks && cd /tmp/lin
python3 -c "open('blocks/blk00000.dat','wb').write(bytes(4096))"
printf '%064d\n' 0 > hashlist.txt
printf 'input=blocks\nhashlist=hashlist.txt\noutput_file=bootstrap.dat\ngenesis=%064d\n' 0 > linearize.cfg
python3 /path/to/bitcoin/contrib/linearize/linearize-data.py linearize.cfg
```

Before, it never returns:

```
Read 1 hashes
Input file blocks/blk00000.dat
<hangs>
```

After:

```
Read 1 hashes
Input file blocks/blk00000.dat
Input file blocks/blk00001.dat
Premature end of block data
```

Indexing a bytes object returns an int in Python 3, so `inhdr[0] == "\0"` is always false and the zero-padding check never fires. The script instead falls through to the magic-bytes search, which advances one byte per iteration; at the end of the file `read(8)` returns 7 bytes and `seek(-7)` moves back to the same offset, so it loops there forever and the `Premature end of block data` path is never reached.

Block files are preallocated in `BLOCKFILE_CHUNK_SIZE` (16 MiB) chunks and only truncated once finalized, so the most recent blk*.dat normally ends in padding.

This is reached whenever the hashlist references blocks that are not in the blocks directory. The most common case is a pruned datadir, which the script explicitly supports - `getFirstBlockFileId()` starts at the first surviving blk file for exactly that reason. The intended response is "Premature end of block data", but that path is never reached.

This is the same one-line change as #32978, which was closed because no reproduction was provided. Happy to add a test to `test/functional/feature_loadblock.py` instead if that is preferred.

The same allowance covers missing undo on AssumeUTXO snapshot chainstates, matching the existing treatment of unavailable snapshot history. Level 4 still reconnects the newer blocks that were disconnected. `verifychain` returns false to indicate incomplete verification. Lower verification levels and corruption checks for undo records marked as present retain their existing behavior.

This came up during [pruned `txindex` review](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36002). The pending `pruneassumevalid` change also needs verification to handle missing undo correctly, so this fix is being split out to land first.

pulls.title: Init pruned empty chainstate
pulls.body:
Fixes #29422

## Motivation

A pruned node can end up with an empty chainstate (the UTXO database) while its
block index already records that the genesis block was pruned. In that state the
node cannot start: an empty chainstate is rebuilt by connecting blocks from
genesis, but the genesis block data is gone, so no tip can ever be connected. On
current master the node waits for a chain tip indefinitely and never prints an
actionable error. (The assertion failure in getBlockHash() reported in #29422
was against an older version; on master it hangs instead.)

How the node reaches this state: during a flush, FlushStateToDisk() writes the
block index before it writes the coins database. If the process is interrupted
between those two writes during the chainstate's first flush, and that flush also
prunes block files, the on-disk block index marks the early blocks (including
genesis) as no longer stored, while the coins database was never written. An OOM
kill during IBD on a low-memory machine is one way to hit this; deleting the
chainstate directory of a pruned node produces the same on-disk state.

## Change

During chainstate initialization, when a chainstate's coins view is empty, check
whether the genesis block is known to the block index but has had its block data
pruned. If so, return ChainstateLoadStatus::FAILURE instead of continuing into
the wait-for-tip path. The existing failure handling then tells the user to
restart with -reindex, and the GUI offers its usual reindex prompt.

Normal startup, a first startup on an empty datadir, and an explicit -reindex are
unaffected, because in those cases the genesis block is not marked as pruned.

The change does not start a reindex automatically, because recovering a pruned
node this way means downloading the whole chain again, which should be the user's
choice.

## Testing

feature_reindex_init.py is extended to reproduce the state directly:

1. Start a node with -fastprune -prune=1.
2. Generate 400 blocks and prune, so genesis block data is removed.
3. Stop the node and delete its chainstate directory.
4. Assert startup fails with the new error instead of hanging.
5. Allow the suggested reindex and assert the node comes back up at height 0.

Without the fix, step 4 never returns and the test hits the 60s startup timeout.

## Verification

Built and tested on macOS arm64 (Apple Clang 17):

```sh
cmake -B build -DENABLE_IPC=OFF
cmake --build build -j10
ctest --test-dir build -j4
python3 build/test/functional/test_runner.py -j10
```

All runnable unit tests passed (script_assets_tests was skipped, its external
test data was not available). The default functional suite passed, as did the
extended pruning/index tests (feature_pruning.py, feature_index_prune.py) and the
assumeutxo tests. No new compiler warnings.

Not tested: Linux/Windows CI, the Qt GUI path, the IPC build, and a real OOM
interruption (the test constructs the resulting on-disk state rather than
triggering an actual OOM).

pulls.title: Prune after coins flush
pulls.body:
# Crash-safe pruning after chainstate persistence

This change makes prune selection non-mutating, then delays block-index pruning and file deletion until after the UTXO cache write. That closes the demonstrated process-crash window where `ReplayBlocks()` needs files that were already deleted. The new order still allows durable prune metadata and deletion to outrun a non-synchronous coins write on machine failure, and it no longer reclaims selected files before the chainstate disk-space preflight. **Watch for:** **confirmed** machine-crash recovery failure and **confirmed** low-disk shutdown regression on the default shared filesystem.

## What this branch solves

This branch addresses one cause of [#29422](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/29422). The issue describes a pruned node restarting with an unusable chainstate after the process was killed during IBD. The reproduced failure happens when pruning deletes block files before the coins database finishes writing. On restart, the older coins database needs those deleted blocks and cannot recover without a full reindex.

The branch changes that order so the block files remain available until the coins write returns. The new test proves that this fixes the **process-crash/OOM-kill path**: unpatched master deletes `blk00000.dat` and fails during restart, while this branch keeps the file and successfully catches up from disk.

It does not repair a node that is already broken; [#36680](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36680) adds that startup detection and recovery message. It also does not yet guarantee safety after a whole-machine crash or power loss, because returning from the coins write does not guarantee that every write is durable on disk.

## High-level view

For process crashes, selected files remain available through the coins transition. The first block-index write protects newly indexed blocks referenced by the coins tip; the second atomically records pruned metadata before unlink, and startup removes files left after that commit.

**Confirmed:** the cross-database durability order is incomplete. Coins batches use LevelDB's non-synchronous mode, while the subsequent block-index prune batch is synchronous, so a machine crash can preserve pruning while losing enough of the coins transition to require the deleted files.

**Confirmed:** the delayed unlink changes minimum free-space behavior. `CheckDiskSpace(datadir, 192 * dirty_count)` now runs while selected block files still occupy the default shared filesystem, so pruning can issue a fatal low-disk error where the previous order first created enough room for the forced coins write.

Manual and automatic pruning use the same new order. Startup retries automatic pruning, while interrupted manual pruning requires another RPC. During assumeutxo background validation, snapshot and historical pruning operate on disjoint height regions backed by separate blockfile cursors.

**Confirmed coverage gap:** the added test reproduces one manual-prune process crash during a partial coins batch. It does not exercise automatic pruning, low disk, machine-level durability, the second block-index commit window, or two live chainstates.

<details>
<summary>Issues (3)</summary>

1. **Unsynced coins transition (confirmed)** — The synchronous prune metadata commit and unlink can survive a machine crash while the preceding non-synchronous coins batches are lost. Pass a prune-specific durable mode through every coins batch, then synchronously commit prune metadata and unlink.
2. **Space reclaimed too late (confirmed)** — On a shared filesystem, the UTXO disk-space check now runs before selected files are removed and can fatally stop a prune that previously made enough room. Pre-prune only files below every live chainstate's replay floor, or reserve the forced coins-write space before block allocation.
3. **Crash-test scope (confirmed)** — The test covers one manual partial-batch process exit and checks only height. Add focused low-disk and automatic-retry cases, compare the recovered UTXO hash, and do not treat this hook as machine-crash durability coverage.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Details</summary>

## Durable prune metadata can outrun the coins database

**Priority 1, confirmed.** The new order treats return from `CoinsTip().Flush()` or `CoinsTip().Sync()` as the durability boundary (`src/validation.cpp:2798-2803`), then synchronously commits the pruned block-index state and deletes the files (`src/validation.cpp:2813-2829`). Both partial and final UTXO batches call `m_db->WriteBatch(batch)` without the sync argument (`src/txdb.cpp:178-180`, `src/txdb.cpp:192-197`), whose default is `fSync = false` (`src/dbwrapper.h:324`). LevelDB states that these writes may be lost when the machine crashes, although they survive a process-only crash (`src/leveldb/include/leveldb/options.h:173-182`).

`BlockTreeDB::WriteBatchSync()` gives the later block-index write a stronger guarantee by calling `WriteBatch(batch, true)` (`src/node/blockstorage.cpp:92-102`). If power is lost after that batch and unlink, the block database can durably record the replay blocks as pruned while the coins database returns at an old tip or with `DB_HEAD_BLOCKS` requiring `ReplayBlocks()`. The replay positions and files are unavailable, recreating the reindex-required failure this change targets.

The smallest viable correction is to pass a durable-prune mode through the coins batch write and use synchronous writes for every partial and final batch when `fFlushForPrune` is true. Commit the prune flag and pruned file/index records in the following synchronous block-index transition, then unlink. The tradeoff is fsync latency during prune-forced flushes rather than every periodic UTXO flush.

## Delayed unlink can prevent pruning on a nearly full shared filesystem

**Priority 2, confirmed.** The added block unlinks at `src/validation.cpp:2829`, after the UTXO preflight at `src/validation.cpp:2798`. That preflight requires `50 MiB + 192 * CoinsTip().GetDirtyCount()` of available space (`src/util/fs_helpers.cpp:94-98`). Block-file allocation only checks that its own allocation leaves the generic 50 MiB reserve (`src/flatfile.cpp:59-70`), which does not reserve the larger forced UTXO write.

On the default shared filesystem, choose free space `F` such that `50 MiB <= F < 50 MiB + 192 * dirty_count`, with selected files large enough to raise `F` above the upper threshold. The old order passed after unlinking; the new order calls `FatalError` before deleting a file. Automatic pruning reaches this order through `FindFilesToPrune()` (`src/validation.cpp:2747-2749`), and manual pruning reaches it through `FindFilesToPruneManual()` (`src/validation.cpp:2740-2744`). Separate block and chainstate filesystems do not benefit from either order.

The smallest crash-safe correction is to split selected files into early-safe and replay-needed sets. Mark files below the replay floor of every live durable chainstate in the first synchronous block-index batch and unlink them before the UTXO space check. Keep files intersecting any old-to-new replay path until the corresponding durable coins flush, then use the second batch and unlink. If no selected file lies outside every replay path, the node must reserve chainstate write space earlier or fail without pruning.

## The second block-index write closes process-crash windows

```text
select files
  -> flush block data
  -> sync current block index
  -> write coins transition
  -> mark selected files pruned in memory
  -> sync pruned file/index records
  -> unlink files
```

A process exit before or during the coins transition leaves block-index positions and files available to `ReplayBlocks()`. An exit after the coins transition but before the second block-index batch leaves an advanced coins database plus a conservative block index and intact files. The second batch atomically writes zeroed `CBlockFileInfo` records and cleared `BLOCK_HAVE_DATA`/`BLOCK_HAVE_UNDO` entries (`src/node/blockstorage.cpp:270-297`, `src/node/blockstorage.cpp:527-544`). If exit occurs after that batch but before or during unlink, startup retries deletion from zero-sized file records (`src/node/blockstorage.cpp:608-623`). A thrown second database write skips unlink, leaving the previous durable index matched with intact files.

The second write is necessary and sufficient for process-crash ordering. It cannot act as a durability barrier for the separate coins database addressed in Priority 1.

## Manual, automatic, and assumeutxo pruning remain separated

Both helpers now only select file numbers (`src/node/blockstorage.cpp:315-325`, `src/node/blockstorage.cpp:357-401`) before converging on the post-coins pruning block (`src/validation.cpp:2740-2753`, `src/validation.cpp:2813-2829`). Automatic selection clears the request flag, but startup calls `PruneAndFlush()` for every chainstate (`src/init.cpp:2043-2051`), which retries target-based pruning after a process crash. The manual target is a sentinel, so an interrupted manual prune waits for another `pruneblockchain` call.

For an unvalidated snapshot, `GetPruneRange()` starts snapshot-chain pruning above the snapshot base (`src/validation.cpp:6381-6386`); the historical chain prunes below its own lagging tip. `BlockfileTypeForHeight()` assigns those regions to separate normal and assumed cursors (`src/node/blockstorage.cpp:787-793`). Each selected range is therefore flushed by the chainstate whose replay can depend on it.

## The crash test covers only the first interrupted coins batch

**Confirmed coverage gap.** The test fixes the mode to manual pruning (`test/functional/feature_prune_crash.py:22-23`) and uses `-dbcrashratio=1` to exit after the first partial coins batch (`test/functional/feature_prune_crash.py:31-39`; hook at `src/txdb.cpp:178-187`). It checks that `blk00000.dat` remains, restart reaches the prior in-memory tip, and a repeated manual prune deletes the file (`test/functional/feature_prune_crash.py:43-54`).

Because LevelDB's non-synchronous writes survive process exit, this hook cannot test machine-crash durability. There is also no hook after the final coins batch or around the second block-index write, no automatic-prune crash case, and no two-chainstate crash case. Add focused coverage for the low-disk preflight and automatic-prune restart path, and compare recovered UTXO state with a reference hash rather than checking only height. Enforce durable ordering in production code because the functional harness cannot reliably emulate lost kernel writeback state.

</details>

<details>
<summary>File map</summary>

- `src/node/blockstorage.cpp`: makes manual and automatic prune discovery selection-only.
- `src/node/blockstorage.h`: documents selection, marking, and unlink responsibilities.
- `src/validation.cpp`: moves prune marking, persistence, and unlink after the coins write and adds the second block-index batch.
- `test/functional/feature_prune_crash.py`: reproduces a manual-prune process crash during a partial coins batch.
- `test/functional/test_runner.py`: registers the new functional test.

Full diff: `git diff upstream/master...HEAD`

</details>

pulls.title: qa: assert_equals -> assert_true/assert_false
pulls.body:
Instead of this in the functional tests:
```python
    assert_equals([long expression pushing next arg to the right], True)
    assert_equals([other long expression pushing next arg to the right], False)
```
we get:
```python
    assert_true([long expression without arg on the right side..])
    assert_false([other long expression without next arg to the right.])
```

The main point of this change is that `assert_true()`/`assert_false()` reduce cognitive tokens when scanning the code (equals to *what*...?). (As a consequence, `assert_true()`/`assert_false()` are also common in other test frameworks).

`assert_equals()` continues to be used in cases where we don't compare to boolean literals.

`assert_true([expression])` is different from plain `assert [expression]` in that `assert` is truthy while `assert_true` requires boolean `True`. (`assert` can also be deactivated when executing Python code in optimized mode (see https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/30529#discussion_r1893029530)).

A smaller scale attempt at introducing `assert_true()` was originally included in #31874 before being dropped.

pulls.title: http: update m_keep_alive under m_send_mutex
pulls.body:
`HTTPRemoteClient::Send()` sets `m_keep_alive` before taking `m_send_mutex` and appending the response to the send buffer, while the I/O thread reads it under `m_send_mutex` in `MaybeSendBytesFromBuffer()` right after the buffer drains to empty. The two updates are therefore not ordered with respect to each other, and a pipelining client can lose a response:

1. Response 1 (keep-alive) is partially sent and the I/O thread is still draining it.
2. Request 2 (`Connection: close`) is parsed from the receive buffer and dispatched to a worker (the send throttle from #36174 only holds a request back once the buffer exceeds `MAX_BODY_SIZE`).
3. The worker clears `m_keep_alive`; the I/O thread then finishes sending response 1, sees an empty buffer with `m_keep_alive == false`, and sets `m_disconnect`.
4. The worker appends response 2, which is dropped when the client is disconnected on the next loop iteration.

This PR moves the assignment into the critical section that appends the response, and turns the field from `std::atomic_bool` into a plain `bool GUARDED_BY(m_send_mutex)` so Clang's thread-safety analysis enforces the ordering (the only reader already holds the mutex). With the flag and the buffer updated together, the I/O thread can no longer observe "empty && !keep_alive" between two pipelined responses.

The ordering dates back to the initial HTTP server implementation (#35182); #35829/#36007 only moved the code. The window is small and `bitcoin-cli` does not pipeline, so this is a low-severity fix.

### Test

`http_pipelined_keepalive_close_tests` reproduces the interleaving deterministically with a mock socket: `Send()` fails with EAGAIN until the second request has been dispatched, then the I/O thread's next `Send()` (made while holding `m_send_mutex`) signals the worker to write its reply, waits for it to reach `HTTPRemoteClient::Send()`, and only then flushes the first reply. Sends are refused again until the test releases them, so the second reply is only delivered if the I/O loop kept the connection open. Without the first commit the test fails with `server.GetConnectionsCount() == 1 has failed [0 != 1]`: the client was disconnected with the second reply still in its send buffer.

pulls.title: kernel: Use typed errors for fatal and flush error notifications
pulls.body:
Part of the libbitcoinkernel project (tracking issue #27587 ), specifically the "Remove translation.h usage from the kernel" item. `kernel::Notifications::fatalError()` and `flushError()` take a `bilingual_str`, which pulls `util/translation.h` and the application-level `G_TRANSLATION_FUN` into the kernel library, and translation is an application concern rather than a consensus one. The same interface already shows the way out: `warningSet()` takes a `kernel::Warning` enum, and the node turns it into a translated string in `node/kernel_notifications.cpp`.

Along with removing the dependency, another goal here is separating responsibilities, because the goals of error handling and error reporting are different: presenting an error to a user is an application concern, not something `libbitcoinkernel` itself should own. The error is structured on both sides: in C++ as the full `kernel::FatalError` variant, and in the C API as its numeric value. With the current changes the C side only carries half of that structure today though, the dynamic fields (a block hash, a path, an exception's `what()`) do not cross the C API yet, even though ideally they should.

This PR does the same for the two error notifications. A new `src/kernel/error.h` defines `kernel::FlushError` as a plain enum and `kernel::FatalError` as a `std::variant` with one struct per error, whose fields carry the context the message needs: a block hash, a path, the `what()` of a caught exception, block heights. It holds types and nothing else, so every message is now built on the node side. The exception is `FatalErrorString()` in `validation.cpp`, because a fatal error raised during validation also fails the block through `BlockValidationState::Error()`, which takes the reason as a plain string right there, and `fatalError()` returns void, so the node has no way to put its message into that state. A follow-up could store the typed error in the state instead and let the node create the string message.

This does not remove the kernel's dependency on `util/translation.h`, it is just a step. The other two notifications, `progress()` and `warningSet()`, still take a `bilingual_str`, and `bitcoinkernel.cpp`, `checks.cpp`, `node/chainstate.cpp`, `txmempool.cpp` and `validation.cpp` still include the header.

There is one behavior change to mention here. The two C API callbacks lose their `message` parameter, so they now carry only the error code, the same pattern that `btck_BlockValidationResult` already uses.

pulls.title: p2p: Reconsider package transactions that are immediately trimmed
pulls.body:
In-master, if a package is entered into mempool at the lowerst chunk feerate, pushing the mempool oversize, this causes that transaction (package) to be trimmed immediately. This is fine and expected, but the returned validation result `TX_MEMPOOL_POLICY` precludes the now-evicted parent from being considered again (i.e. fetched / processed as package) until after another block is found.

This is not a major issue, but would result in unneeded censorship of someone low-balling package feerates.

The already-in-mempool case needs a bit more logic due to the `FeeFailure`'s requirement of package feerate knowledge, so I opted to use the "would have used" value even though it was never directly submitted in the same-txid-different-wtxid case. **Alternatively**, we could simply get rid of the `FeeFailure` value as IIUC it's not used in non-testing code. This may be a larger code change but could make the resulting code more maintainable going forward. This could also be future work.

Related to finding made by Loupe, and subsequently Red Team.

pulls.title: qt: don't abort or drop settings when dynamic settings are disabled
pulls.body:
`ArgsManager::WriteSettingsFile` throws when dynamic settings are disabled, and three call sites in `NodeImpl` call it without checking first. So `bitcoin-qt -nosettings` aborts on `-resetguisettings`, and on the legacy GUI settings migration when an old Qt setting is still present, which comes back on every start because the abort happens before the key is removed.

The fourth call site in that file is the wallet path in `ChainImpl`, and #36176 guards it. These three are the options dialog, and I ran into them while testing that PR.

The flag is easier to reach than it looks, since the fatal error box suggests `-nosettings` when the settings file cannot be written.

Guarding the writes on its own is not enough, because three things then happen silently instead of aborting. The migration drops the legacy keys, since it removes them whether or not the write landed. The dialog closes reporting success, since `setOption` only reported parse errors and `QDataWidgetMapper::submit()` does not propagate what `setData` returns. And it asks for a restart that would discard the change rather than apply it, which is reachable today without the flag.

`bitcoin-qt -regtest -nosettings -resetguisettings` aborts on master and starts here. The Qt tests cover the guards and each of those, with settings disabled and with a write that fails, and each one fails without its change.

The second commit reports rather than fixes the abort, so it can be dropped if reviewers would rather keep this to the crash.

pulls.title: test: cover Taproot standardness rules in mempool_accept
pulls.body:
`IsWitnessStandard` rejects tapscript stack items over 80 bytes and an empty control block, and no test asserts `bad-witness-nonstandard` for either. With the 80-byte check removed, `feature_taproot.py` failed on only 6 of the ten seeds I tried, and with the empty control block check removed it can't fail at all, since none of its spenders has an empty control block. Without that check the node segfaults reading `control_block[0]`.

This adds a case for each to `mempool_accept.py`, by mutating the witness of the P2TR script-path spend the file already builds. Each case fails with its `policy.cpp` branch disabled and passes with it restored.

pulls.title: validation: don't accept txs to the mempool while loading a snapshot
pulls.body:
`ActivateSnapshot` checks that the mempool is empty before it starts, but `PopulateAndValidateSnapshot` then runs without `cs_main`, which takes minutes on mainnet. A transaction entering the mempool in that window (e.g. through `sendrawtransaction`) hits the assert in `AddChainstate`:

```
Assertion failed: (!prev_chainstate.m_mempool || prev_chainstate.m_mempool->size() == 0), function AddChainstate, file validation.cpp, line 6201.
```

By then the base blockhash file has been written, so the node needs `-reindex` to start again.

This sets a flag on `ChainstateManager` while `ActivateSnapshot` runs, and `AcceptToMemoryPool` and `ProcessNewPackage` reject with `snapshot-loading` while it's set. `testmempoolaccept` still works. A second `loadtxoutset` started while one is running is also rejected.

`test_mempool_blocked_during_load` in `feature_assumeutxo.py` pauses the load through a FIFO, checks that `sendrawtransaction` and `submitpackage` are rejected and the mempool stays empty, then lets the load finish. On master the transaction is accepted and the node aborts. The test is skipped where `os.mkfifo` isn't available.

pulls.title: net: Use exclusive P2P listen sockets on Windows
pulls.body:
on Windows, `SO_REUSEADDR` does not carry over the same semantics as on
POSIX systems. a second socket can set `SO_REUSEADDR` and bind to a
port that is _already in use_ by another process running under
the _same_ user account. this means another local process could bind to
the P2P listen port and receive incoming connections intended for
`bitcoind`.

this matters because the P2P listener is expected to have exclusive
ownership of its address and port. allowing another process to bind to
it could let that process _intercept_ incoming P2P connections. this is
in a similar spirit to #36169, which made the RPC listener exclusive on
Windows.

to fix this, we use `SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE` for the P2P listen socket on
Windows instead of `SO_REUSEADDR`, while retaining `SO_REUSEADDR` on
other platforms. the added test verifies the expected behaviour by
attempting to bind a second socket to the same port. on Windows, this
fails with `WSAEACCES` (`10013`), which Python exposes as
`PermissionError` (an `OSError` subclass).

references:

- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/winsock/using-so-reuseaddr-and-so-exclusiveaddruse
- https://stackoverflow.com/questions/14388706/how-do-so-reuseaddr-and-so-reuseport-differ/14388707#14388707
